title: Visiting the sites
hook: gurdwaras now mark Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Khalsa shall rule: a couplet heard as sovereignty, as gentle rule, and as ruling the self. Your line was rule yourself first. What did you take charge of? Day eight hundred eighty-two.

Flat fields. Wheat, or mustard in its season, running to the edge of sight. An irrigation channel, a dirt road, a tractor parked by a wall. And in the middle of it, a white building with a dome and a tall flagpole, the saffron Nishan Sahib lifting in the wind. If you didn't know the story, you'd see a village gurdwara like any other. But this ground has a name in Sikh memory. Two places like this are where today goes. Today: visiting the sites.
screen: `FLAT FIELDS, A DIRT ROAD.` → `A WHITE DOME, A SAFFRON FLAG.` → `GROUND WITH A NAME IN MEMORY.`

segments.voice: The first place is Kahnuwan, near the marshes where, a few weeks back on this path, the families and riders were trapped in the smaller holocaust, the chhota ghallughara. Ghallughara means a great destruction. Chhota means small, though nothing about it was small to the people who lived it. Today a gurdwara stands there, and Sikhs come to remember. The second place is Kup Rahira, where the Khalsa made a moving ring around its families and the great holocaust, the vadda ghallughara, fell on them. A gurdwara marks that ground too. Those are the two facts. Now the meaning. Notice what stands at the heart of each site. Not a battle trophy. Not a wall of grievance. A gurdwara: a place where the Guru Granth Sahib is opened, hymns are sung, and a langar feeds anyone who walks in. The memorial is a working kitchen. That fits everything this week has been about: memory pointed at courage, the pot before the sword. And there's a quiet lesson in the sites themselves. The fields came back. Crops grow right up to the gurdwara walls. A child can grow up within sight of the gurdwara and learn the story from the person who serves them tea there. The places hold what happened so that the people who live there don't have to carry it alone. This week: Rattan Singh Bhangu, remembering without hatred, the Budha Dal today, daily life on horseback, langar in hard times, the Khalsa shall rule, and visiting the sites. The places remember.
screen: `KAHNUWAN: THE SMALLER HOLOCAUST.` · `KUP RAHIRA: THE GREAT HOLOCAUST.` · `NOT A MONUMENT, A GURDWARA.` · `THE FIELDS CAME BACK.` · then, large: `THE PLACES REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a map. If you have a phone nearby, open a map and search for Kahnuwan, or Kup Rahira. Don't read anything. Just find it. Zoom in until you can see the fields, the roads, the shape of the village. Then put the phone down, close your eyes, and breathe. Hold the picture of that ordinary ground and what tradition says happened there. If you can't look it up, hold the picture of the white dome in the fields. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Visiting the sites. Gurdwaras now stand at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira, where the two holocausts fell, with scripture, song and a kitchen. Today's word.
Your line: the places remember. Today, find out about one place near you where something hard happened, and what stands there now. Day eight hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras stand at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira; Sikhs visit to pray and remember the two ghallugharas, and the anniversaries are marked there with readings, kirtan and langar.

original.note: Gurmukhi for ghallughara, a great destruction, the word Sikhs use for the two holocausts.

trapdoor: what you thought: old battlefields are fenced off and silent.
what it means: at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira, gurdwaras stand in working fields, with scripture, song and langar.
what a scholar hears: Sikh memory marks its sites of suffering with living gurdwaras, so remembrance happens through worship and a shared meal at the center, not only a battle monument.
